Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Within the elastic limit, the elastic potential energy stored per unit volume of a stretched wire is ½ × stress × strain.
Statement II: For the same tensile stress, a wire of a material with a larger Young's modulus stores more elastic energy per unit volume.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: The work done in stretching a wire is ½Fl, so the energy per unit volume is ½(F/A)(l/L) = ½ × stress × strain: Statement I is true. With strain = stress/Y, the energy density is stress²/(2Y), so at the same stress a larger Y gives LESS stored energy per unit volume: Statement II is false.
steps: u = ½ σ ε (Statement I, true)
u = σ²/(2Y) → larger Y, smaller u at fixed σ (Statement II, false)
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement II would be right for the same STRAIN (u = ½Yε²), not for the same stress.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Mechanical Properties of Solids', elastic potential energy in a stretched wire
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Newton's law of cooling, that the rate of loss of heat is proportional to the temperature difference between a body and its surroundings, holds for small temperature differences.
Statement II: A body cooling according to Newton's law takes longer to cool through 10 °C when its temperature is closer to that of the surroundings.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: NCERT states the law for a small temperature difference between the body and its surroundings, so Statement I is true. Since −dT/dt = k(T − T₀), the rate of cooling is smaller when T is closer to T₀, so the same 10 °C drop takes more time near the surrounding temperature. Statement II is true.
steps: Statement I: law valid for small (T − T₀) → true
Statement II: rate ∝ (T − T₀) → slower cooling near T₀ → more time → true
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements are true; Statement II follows from the law, since the cooling rate falls as the temperature difference falls.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Thermal Properties of Matter', Newton's law of cooling
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A small metal sphere falls through a viscous liquid with its terminal velocity, and the viscous force on it dissipates energy at the rate P. A sphere of the same metal with twice the radius falls through the same liquid with its terminal velocity. Assuming Stokes' law holds, the rate at which the viscous force dissipates energy on the second sphere is:

solution.explanation: At terminal velocity v = 2r²(ρ − σ)g/(9η), so v ∝ r². The viscous force equals the weight minus the buoyancy, 6πηrv ∝ r³. The power dissipated is F v ∝ r³ × r² = r⁵.
solution.why_others_wrong: 16P takes F ∝ r²; 8P gives only the change in the force; 4P gives only the change in the terminal velocity.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Mechanical Properties of Fluids', Stokes' law and terminal velocity
solution.final_answer: Option D: 32P

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A steady, smooth stream of water comes vertically down out of a tap whose opening has a radius of 1 cm, with a speed of 1 m/s at the opening. Taking g = 10 m/s² and neglecting viscosity, air resistance and surface tension, the radius of the stream 15 cm below the opening is:

solution.concept: Free fall combined with the equation of continuity
solution.explanation: Each element of water falls freely, so its speed grows as v² = v₀² + 2gh. The same volume flows through every cross-section per second, so Av is constant and the stream narrows.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1/2 cm takes r ∝ 1/v instead of A ∝ 1/v; 1/4 cm uses the ratio of v² for the radius; √2 cm assumes the stream widens as it speeds up.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Mechanical Properties of Fluids', streamline flow (equation of continuity)
solution.final_answer: Option C: 1/√2 cm

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Two solid spheres of the same material, with radii in the ratio 1 : 2, have the same surface finish and are at the same temperature, in the same surroundings, losing heat only by radiation. The ratio of their initial rates of fall of temperature (smaller sphere : larger sphere) is:

solution.concept: Rate of cooling by radiation depends on area/heat capacity
solution.explanation: The rate of heat loss by radiation is proportional to the surface area (same T, same surroundings, same surface). The fall of temperature is this rate divided by the heat capacity mc, which is proportional to the volume. So dT/dt ∝ r²/r³ = 1/r.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1 : 2 inverts the ratio; 4 : 1 uses only the ratio of the areas inverted (1/r²); 1 : 1 assumes that the same temperature means the same rate of cooling.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Thermal Properties of Matter', radiation; specific heat capacity
solution.final_answer: Option B: 2 : 1

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): During a long spell of very cold weather, a deep lake freezes at its surface while the water near its bottom stays liquid, at about 4 °C.
Reason (R): Water has its maximum density at about 4 °C, so as the lake cools, water at 4 °C sinks to the bottom while the colder, less dense water stays at the top and freezes there.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.explanation: Most liquids become denser as they cool, but water contracts only down to about 4 °C and expands on further cooling. As a lake cools, surface water sinks until the whole lake is near 4 °C; after that, colder water is lighter and stays on top, where it freezes. The ice and the cold surface layer insulate the water below, which stays liquid near 4 °C, allowing aquatic life to survive. R is the reason for A.
steps: Water at 4 °C collects at the bottom; colder water stays on top
Freezing starts at the surface; the bottom stays near 4 °C → A true, R explains it
solution.why_others_wrong: R is the cause of A, not a separate fact, so B is wrong; both statements are true, so C and D are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Thermal Properties of Matter', thermal expansion (anomalous expansion of water)
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
A wire 1.5 m long, of cross-sectional area 0.5 mm² and Young's modulus 1 × 10¹¹ N/m², hangs from a rigid support and carries a load that exerts a force of 50 N on it. Within the elastic limit, which of the following statements are correct?

(a) The tensile stress in the wire is 1 × 10⁸ N/m².
(b) The longitudinal strain is 1 × 10⁻³.
(c) The extension of the wire is 1.5 mm.
(d) The elastic potential energy stored in the wire is 75 mJ.
(e) A wire of the same material and length but twice the diameter, carrying the same load, would extend by 0.75 mm.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Stress, strain, extension and stored energy of a wire
solution.explanation: Stress = F/A, strain = stress/Y, extension = strain × L, and the energy stored = ½ × F × extension. Doubling the diameter makes the area 4 times, so the extension falls to one quarter.
steps: (d) U = ½ × 50 × 1.5 × 10⁻³ = 37.5 mJ, not 75 mJ → false
(e) area × 4 → extension 1.5/4 = 0.375 mm, not 0.75 mm → false
solution.why_others_wrong: (d) forgets the ½ in U = ½F·Δl; (e) treats the area as proportional to the diameter instead of its square.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Mechanical Properties of Solids', Young's modulus; elastic potential energy in a stretched wire
solution.final_answer: Option D: (a), (b) and (c) only

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A gas enclosed in a cylinder is said to be in thermodynamic equilibrium when:

options.text: Its temperature is 0 °C and its pressure is 1 atm
Its macroscopic variables, such as pressure, volume, temperature, mass and composition, do not change with time

solution.explanation: NCERT: a system is in thermodynamic equilibrium if the macroscopic variables that characterise it do not change in time. Its molecules keep moving randomly; equilibrium is a property of the macroscopic state, not of any particular values of P and T.
steps: Equilibrium → P, V, T, mass and composition constant in time
solution.why_others_wrong: Molecular motion never stops in a gas at any real temperature; equilibrium can occur at any pressure and temperature; the internal energy of a gas in equilibrium is not zero.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Thermodynamics', thermal equilibrium
solution.final_answer: Option C: Its macroscopic variables, such as pressure, volume, temperature, mass and composition, do not change with time

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (term used in thermodynamics) with List-II (its meaning).

List-I:
A. Diathermic wall
B. Adiabatic wall
C. Heat reservoir
D. Cyclic process

List-II:
I. A body so large that its temperature does not change appreciably when heat flows into or out of it
II. A process in which the system returns to its initial state
III. A conducting wall that allows heat to flow through it
IV. An insulating wall that does not allow heat to flow through it

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: A diathermic (conducting) wall lets heat pass; an adiabatic (insulating) wall does not. A heat reservoir is so large that its temperature stays fixed while it exchanges heat. In a cyclic process the system comes back to its initial state.
steps: Cyclic process → returns to initial state (II)
solution.why_others_wrong: The wrong codes exchange the two kinds of wall, or the reservoir with the cyclic process.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Thermodynamics', thermal equilibrium; thermodynamic processes
solution.final_answer: Option A: A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): No work is done by or on an ideal gas in an isochoric process.
Reason (R): In an isochoric process, the temperature of the gas remains constant.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.explanation: In an isochoric process the volume is constant, so W = ∫P dV = 0: A is true. The heat supplied changes the internal energy and therefore the temperature; it is the isothermal process, not the isochoric one, in which the temperature stays constant. So R is false.
steps: R: Q = ΔU = nC_vΔT ≠ 0 in general → T changes → false
solution.why_others_wrong: R describes an isothermal process, so options A and B are wrong; A is true, so D is wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Thermodynamics', thermodynamic processes (isochoric process)
solution.final_answer: Option C: A is true but R is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: An ideal gas is taken from state A (pressure 1 × 10⁵ Pa, volume 1 L) to state B (pressure 2 × 10⁵ Pa, volume 2 L) by two different paths. Path 1: first at constant volume to 2 × 10⁵ Pa, then at constant pressure to 2 L. Path 2: first at constant pressure to 2 L, then at constant volume to 2 × 10⁵ Pa. The heat absorbed along path 1 exceeds that absorbed along path 2 by:

solution.concept: Heat depends on the path; internal energy does not
solution.explanation: Both paths join the same two states, so ΔU is the same. By the first law Q = ΔU + W, so the difference in heat equals the difference in the work done by the gas, which is the area under each path on the P–V diagram.
steps: Path 1: W₁ = (2 × 10⁵)(1 × 10⁻³) = 200 J (expansion at the higher pressure)
solution.why_others_wrong: Zero assumes heat is a state function like U; 200 J and 300 J give the work along path 1 alone or the sum of the two works.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Thermodynamics', first law of thermodynamics; state variables
solution.final_answer: Option B: 100 J

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Two identical samples of an ideal gas start from the same state (P, V, T). One expands reversibly at constant pressure to volume 2V; the other expands reversibly and isothermally to volume 2V. Taking ln 2 = 0.693, the ratio of the work done by the gas at constant pressure to that done isothermally is about:

solution.concept: Work in isobaric and isothermal expansions
solution.explanation: At constant pressure W₁ = P(2V − V) = PV. Isothermally W₂ = nRT ln(2V/V) = PV ln 2, since nRT = PV at the start. The ratio is 1/ln 2.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.69 is the inverse ratio; 1 assumes equal work for the same change of volume; 2 compares the final volumes instead of the work.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Thermodynamics', thermodynamic processes (isothermal and isobaric)
solution.final_answer: Option D: 1.44

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The molar specific heat of a gas at constant pressure is greater than that at constant volume because, at constant pressure, part of the heat supplied is used in doing work as the gas expands.
Statement II: The specific heat capacity of a gas is not unique: it depends on the process by which heat is supplied to it.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Specific heat capacities of a gas
solution.explanation: At constant volume all the heat raises the internal energy. At constant pressure the gas also expands and does work, so more heat is needed for the same rise in temperature: C_p > C_v (C_p − C_v = R for an ideal gas). Statement I is true. Because the heat needed depends on how much work is done, the specific heat depends on the process: Statement II is true.
steps: Statement I: Q_p = ΔU + PΔV > Q_v = ΔU → true
Statement II: heat for a given ΔT depends on the process → true
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements are true. Statement II is the general point, Statement I a particular case of it.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Thermodynamics', specific heat capacity
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Three moles of a monatomic ideal gas in a closed rigid vessel are heated from 300 K to 320 K. Taking R = 8.3 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, which of the following statements are correct?

(a) No work is done by the gas.
(b) The internal energy of the gas increases by 747 J.
(c) The heat supplied to the gas is 747 J.
(d) The final pressure of the gas is 16/15 of its initial pressure.
(e) If the same gas were heated at constant pressure through the same 20 K, it would also need 747 J of heat.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: First law in an isochoric process
solution.explanation: A rigid vessel keeps the volume fixed, so W = 0 and Q = ΔU = nC_vΔT. At constant volume P ∝ T. At constant pressure the gas would also do work, so more heat, nC_pΔT, would be needed.
solution.why_others_wrong: (e) forgets the work done during expansion at constant pressure. Options leaving out (a) or (d), or including (e), are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Thermodynamics', first law of thermodynamics; specific heat capacity
solution.final_answer: Option B: (a), (b), (c) and (d) only

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A diatomic ideal gas (rigid molecules) is enclosed in a vertical cylinder by a smooth piston of mass 10 kg and area 0.01 m². The atmospheric pressure is 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa and g = 10 m/s². The gas is heated slowly, and the piston rises through 0.2 m. The heat supplied to the gas is:

solution.concept: First law with a constant-pressure expansion against a loaded piston
solution.explanation: The piston moves slowly, so the gas pressure stays equal to atmospheric pressure plus the piston's weight per unit area: an isobaric process. For a diatomic gas at constant pressure, Q = nC_pΔT = (7/2)nRΔT = (7/2)PΔV.
solution.why_others_wrong: 220 J is only the work done by the gas; 550 J is only the rise in internal energy; 700 J leaves out the piston's weight in the pressure.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Thermodynamics', first law of thermodynamics; isobaric process
solution.final_answer: Option C: 770 J

questions.subject: Physics
questions.subtopic: Second law, reversible and irreversible processes
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Real thermodynamic processes can at best approximate a reversible process, which is an idealisation.
Reason (R): In real processes there are dissipative effects, such as friction and viscosity, and heat flows across finite temperature differences, so the system and surroundings cannot both be restored exactly.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.explanation: A reversible process must be quasi-static and free of dissipative effects; only then can it be retraced with both system and surroundings returning to their original states. Every real process involves some friction, viscosity or finite-rate heat flow, which is why it is irreversible and why the reversible process is only an idealisation. R gives exactly this reason.
steps: Real processes always have dissipation → irreversible
solution.why_others_wrong: R is the cause of A, not an unrelated fact, so B is wrong; both statements are true, so C and D are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Thermodynamics', reversible and irreversible processes
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Two moles of a diatomic ideal gas (rigid molecules) are taken from 300 K to 400 K along a process that is a straight line passing through the origin on a volume–temperature (V–T) graph. Taking R = 8.3 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, which of the following statements are correct?

(a) The pressure of the gas stays constant.
(b) The work done by the gas is 1660 J.
(c) The heat absorbed by the gas is 5810 J.
(d) The internal energy of the gas increases by 1660 J.
(e) The density of the gas increases during the process.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Reading a process from a V–T graph
solution.explanation: V ∝ T means V/T is constant, which by PV = nRT means P is constant: an isobaric process. Then W = PΔV = nRΔT, ΔU = nC_vΔT with C_v = (5/2)R, and Q = nC_pΔT with C_p = (7/2)R.
steps: (e) volume increases at fixed mass → density decreases → false
solution.why_others_wrong: (d) gives the work done instead of the change in internal energy; (e) has the wrong direction, since the gas expands as it is heated at constant pressure.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Thermodynamics', first law of thermodynamics; isobaric process
solution.final_answer: Option D: (a), (b) and (c) only

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: An ideal gas is kept in a closed rigid container. If the speed of every one of its molecules were doubled, the pressure of the gas would become:

solution.explanation: P = (1/3)nm⟨v²⟩. In a rigid closed container n (molecules per unit volume) and m are fixed, so P ∝ ⟨v²⟩. Doubling every speed makes ⟨v²⟩ four times. (Each collision transfers twice the momentum, and collisions happen twice as often.)
solution.why_others_wrong: 2 times counts only the larger momentum per collision (or takes P ∝ v); √2 times confuses the result with the rms speed when T doubles; 8 times uses P ∝ v³.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Kinetic Theory', pressure of an ideal gas
solution.final_answer: Option C: 4 times

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: According to the kinetic theory of gases, the absolute temperature of an ideal gas is directly proportional to:

options.text: The average translational kinetic energy of its molecules
The rms speed of its molecules
The total linear momentum of its molecules
The number of molecules in the gas

solution.explanation: Kinetic theory gives the average translational kinetic energy of a molecule as (3/2)k_BT, so T is directly proportional to it. The rms speed is proportional to √T, not to T.
solution.why_others_wrong: The rms speed varies as √T; the total momentum of a gas at rest in its container is zero on average; temperature does not depend on how many molecules there are.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Kinetic Theory', kinetic interpretation of temperature
solution.final_answer: Option A: The average translational kinetic energy of its molecules

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A vessel of volume 2 L contains a gas at a pressure of 2 atm and another vessel of volume 3 L contains the same gas at 1 atm, both at the same temperature. The vessels are connected by a narrow tube of negligible volume and the temperature is kept the same. Treating the gas as ideal, the final common pressure is:

solution.concept: Ideal gas equation: conservation of the number of moles
solution.explanation: At a fixed temperature, the number of moles in each vessel is proportional to PV. The total number of moles does not change when the vessels are joined, so P_f(V₁ + V₂) = P₁V₁ + P₂V₂.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.5 atm is the simple average of the pressures; 3 atm adds the pressures; 1.6 atm weights each pressure by the wrong volume (2 × 3 + 1 × 2)/5.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Kinetic Theory', behaviour of gases (ideal gas equation)
solution.final_answer: Option D: 1.4 atm

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Helium is a monatomic gas of molar mass 4 g/mol. Using the law of equipartition of energy and taking R = 8.3 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, the specific heat capacity of helium at constant volume (per unit mass) is about:

solution.concept: From molar specific heat to specific heat per unit mass
solution.explanation: A monatomic molecule has 3 translational degrees of freedom, so U = (3/2)RT per mole and C_v = (3/2)R per mole. Dividing by the molar mass in kg/mol gives the value per kilogram.
solution.why_others_wrong: 12.5 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ is the MOLAR value with the wrong unit; 5.2 × 10³ J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ is c_p, from (5/2)R; 3.1 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ divides by 4 instead of 0.004 kg/mol.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Kinetic Theory', law of equipartition of energy; specific heat capacity
solution.final_answer: Option B: 3.1 × 10³ J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (gas molecule) with List-II (number of quadratic terms in its energy that share the energy, each contributing ½k_BT on average, according to the law of equipartition of energy).

List-I:
A. Helium (monatomic)
B. Nitrogen (N₂) with rigid molecules
C. Nitrogen (N₂) whose molecules also vibrate in one mode
D. A rigid non-linear polyatomic molecule

List-II:
I. 6
II. 3
III. 7
IV. 5

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Equipartition of energy and degrees of freedom
solution.explanation: Translational motion gives 3 terms; a rigid diatomic (linear) molecule adds 2 rotational terms; a rigid non-linear molecule adds 3. A vibrational mode adds 2 terms (kinetic and potential energy), i.e. k_BT.
solution.why_others_wrong: The wrong codes count a vibrational mode as one term instead of two, or give a linear molecule three rotational terms.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Kinetic Theory', law of equipartition of energy
solution.final_answer: Option C: A-II, B-IV, C-III, D-I

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: An ideal gas of rigid diatomic molecules (γ = 7/5) has an rms molecular speed v. It is compressed reversibly and adiabatically to 1/32 of its volume. The rms speed of its molecules becomes:

solution.concept: Adiabatic compression and the rms speed
solution.explanation: In a reversible adiabatic process TV^(γ−1) is constant, so the temperature rises by 32^(2/5). The rms speed is proportional to √T.
solution.why_others_wrong: 4v gives the factor for the temperature, not the speed; √2 v uses the exponent 1/5 instead of 2/5, so T only doubles; 32v treats the speed as proportional to the compression ratio.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Kinetic Theory', kinetic interpretation of temperature; 'Thermodynamics', adiabatic process
solution.final_answer: Option A: 2v

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Equal masses of hydrogen (H₂) and oxygen (O₂), both treated as ideal gases of rigid diatomic molecules, have equal internal energies at the same temperature.
Reason (R): At a given temperature, the average energy of a rigid diatomic molecule is (5/2)k_BT, the same for H₂ and O₂.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Internal energy depends on the number of molecules
solution.explanation: R is true by the law of equipartition (3 translational + 2 rotational terms). But equal masses contain very different numbers of molecules: with molar masses 2 g/mol and 32 g/mol, the hydrogen sample has 16 times as many molecules, so 16 times the internal energy. So A is false.
steps: R: energy per molecule = (5/2)k_BT for both → true
solution.why_others_wrong: A is false, so options A, B and C are wrong. Equal energy per molecule does not mean equal energy per unit mass.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Kinetic Theory', law of equipartition of energy
solution.final_answer: Option D: A is false but R is true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A particle executes simple harmonic motion with an amplitude of 5 cm and a period of 2 s. Its average speed over one complete oscillation is:

solution.concept: Distance covered in one period of SHM
solution.explanation: In one complete oscillation the particle goes from the mean position to one extreme, back, to the other extreme and back: a distance of 4A. Average speed = total distance / time.
solution.why_others_wrong: Zero is the average VELOCITY over a period (the displacement is zero); 5π cm/s is the maximum speed Aω; 5 cm/s counts only 2A per period.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Oscillations', simple harmonic motion
solution.final_answer: Option B: 10 cm/s

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Two particles execute simple harmonic motions given by x₁ = A sin(ωt + π/6) and x₂ = A cos ωt along the same line. The phase difference between the two motions is:

solution.concept: Comparing phases: writing cosine as a sine
solution.explanation: To compare phases, write both motions with the same function: A cos ωt = A sin(ωt + π/2). The phase difference is then the difference of the phase constants.
steps: Δφ = π/2 − π/6 = π/3 (x₂ leads x₁)
solution.why_others_wrong: π/6 compares cos ωt with sin ωt as if they were in phase; 2π/3 adds the phase constants; π/2 is the difference between sine and cosine alone, ignoring the π/6.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Oscillations', simple harmonic motion (phase)
solution.final_answer: Option D: π/3

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: In a stationary wave set up on a stretched string at a frequency of 500 Hz, adjacent nodes are 20 cm apart. The speed of the travelling waves on the string is:

solution.concept: Node spacing in a stationary wave
solution.explanation: Adjacent nodes in a stationary wave are half a wavelength apart, so λ = 2 × 20 cm = 0.40 m. The speed of the travelling waves is v = fλ.
solution.why_others_wrong: 100 m/s takes the node spacing as a whole wavelength; 400 m/s takes it as a quarter wavelength (the node-to-antinode distance); 20 m/s converts 20 cm wrongly to 0.02 m.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Waves', reflection of waves (standing waves and normal modes)
solution.final_answer: Option B: 200 m/s

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Which of the following motions is periodic but NOT oscillatory?

options.text: The bob of a simple pendulum swinging through a small angle
A block oscillating on a horizontal spring
A particle moving uniformly along a circle
A prong of a vibrating tuning fork

solution.explanation: NCERT: every oscillatory motion is periodic, but not every periodic motion is oscillatory. Uniform circular motion repeats itself after a fixed time, but the particle does not move to and fro about a mean position.
steps: Periodic → repeats after a fixed interval
Oscillatory → to-and-fro about a mean position
Uniform circular motion: periodic, not oscillatory
solution.why_others_wrong: A pendulum bob, a block on a spring and a tuning-fork prong all move to and fro about a mean position, so their motions are both periodic and oscillatory.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Oscillations', periodic and oscillatory motions
solution.final_answer: Option C: A particle moving uniformly along a circle

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: When a transverse wave passes from a light string into a heavier string joined to it, under the same tension, its frequency stays the same while its speed and wavelength decrease.
Statement II: In a sound wave travelling through air, a compression is a region where the density and the pressure of the air are higher than normal.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Wave speed, frequency and wavelength; compressions
solution.explanation: The frequency of a wave is set by the source and does not change at a boundary. The speed on a string is √(T/μ), so a larger μ means a smaller speed, and λ = v/f is smaller too: Statement I is true. In a longitudinal wave, compressions are regions of higher density and pressure, rarefactions of lower: Statement II is true.
steps: Statement I: f fixed, v = √(T/μ) falls as μ rises, λ = v/f falls → true
Statement II: compression = higher density and pressure → true
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements are true.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Waves', speed of a travelling wave; transverse and longitudinal waves
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A particle starts from its mean position at t = 0 and executes simple harmonic motion with a period of 2 s. The earliest time at which its kinetic energy equals its potential energy is:

solution.concept: Energy sharing in SHM and the corresponding time
solution.explanation: K = U when each is half the total energy: ½kx² = ¼kA², so x = A/√2. With x = A sin(2πt/T), this first happens at 2πt/T = π/4, i.e. t = T/8.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.5 s (T/4) is the time to reach the extreme position; 0.125 s (T/16) halves the phase angle; 0.33 s (T/6) is the time to reach x = A/2, where K = 3U.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Oscillations', energy in simple harmonic motion
solution.final_answer: Option B: 0.25 s

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Tuning fork P of frequency 256 Hz and tuning fork Q produce 6 beats per second when sounded together. When the prongs of Q are filed slightly, the two forks produce 4 beats per second. The frequency of Q before filing was:

solution.concept: Beats, and the effect of filing a tuning fork
solution.explanation: Beat frequency = |f_P − f_Q|, so f_Q is 250 Hz or 262 Hz. Filing the prongs makes them lighter, which RAISES the frequency of the fork. If f_Q were 262 Hz, raising it would increase the beat frequency; since the beats fall to 4 per second, f_Q must have been 250 Hz (raised to 252 Hz).
steps: 250 → 252 Hz gives 4 beats/s (matches); 262 → higher gives more than 6 beats/s
solution.why_others_wrong: 262 Hz assumes filing lowers the frequency (that is the effect of loading with wax); 252 Hz is the frequency after filing; 260 Hz uses the second beat count with the wrong sign.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Waves', beats
solution.final_answer: Option C: 250 Hz

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A string 1.5 m long is fixed at both ends. Transverse waves travel on it at 300 m/s. When it vibrates in a normal mode of frequency 500 Hz, the number of nodes on it, including the two fixed ends, is:

solution.concept: Normal modes of a string fixed at both ends
solution.explanation: The normal modes have L = nλ/2, i.e. fₙ = nv/(2L). The nth mode has n loops, and therefore n + 1 nodes counting the two ends.
solution.why_others_wrong: 5 is the number of loops (antinodes), not nodes; 4 leaves out both ends; 10 counts the number of half wavelengths in a doubled length.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Waves', standing waves and normal modes
solution.final_answer: Option B: 6

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
For a particle executing simple harmonic motion about x = 0 between x = −A and x = +A, match List-I (graph) with List-II (its shape).

List-I:
A. Velocity v against displacement x
B. Acceleration a against displacement x
C. Potential energy U against displacement x
D. Total mechanical energy E against displacement x

List-II:
I. A horizontal straight line
II. An ellipse
III. A straight line through the origin with a negative slope
IV. A parabola opening upward with its minimum at x = 0

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Graphs of SHM quantities against displacement
solution.explanation: v = ±ω√(A² − x²) gives v²/(ωA)² + x²/A² = 1, an ellipse. a = −ω²x is a straight line of negative slope through the origin. U = ½kx² is a parabola with its minimum at the mean position. E = ½kA² is the same at every x.
steps: B: a = −ω²x → straight line, negative slope (III)
D: E = ½kA² constant → horizontal line (I)
solution.why_others_wrong: The wrong codes swap the velocity graph with the acceleration graph, or the potential energy with the total energy.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Oscillations', velocity and acceleration in SHM; energy in SHM
solution.final_answer: Option D: A-II, B-III, C-IV, D-I

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): For a particle executing simple harmonic motion, the speed is greatest at the extreme positions.
Reason (R): At the extreme positions of simple harmonic motion, the restoring force and the acceleration have their greatest magnitudes.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.explanation: v = ω√(A² − x²) is zero at the extremes (x = ±A) and greatest at the mean position, so A is false. a = −ω²x has its greatest magnitude ω²A at the extremes, so R is true.
steps: A: at x = ±A, v = 0 → speed least, not greatest → false
R: |a| = ω²|x| greatest at |x| = A → true
solution.why_others_wrong: A is false, so options A, B and C are wrong. A large acceleration does not mean a large speed: at the extremes the particle is momentarily at rest.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Oscillations', velocity and acceleration in simple harmonic motion
solution.final_answer: Option D: A is false but R is true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A block of mass 3 kg attached to a light horizontal spring oscillates on a smooth floor with amplitude A. Just as the block passes through its mean position, a lump of putty of mass 1 kg is dropped vertically onto it and sticks. The new amplitude of oscillation is:

solution.concept: SHM combined with conservation of momentum
solution.explanation: The putty has no horizontal velocity, so horizontal momentum is conserved: the speed at the mean position drops from v₀ = Aω to 3v₀/4. The angular frequency also changes, to ω' = √(k/4) = ω√(3/4). The new amplitude is the new maximum speed divided by ω'.
solution.shortcut: A' = A√(M/(M + m)) when mass is added at the mean position.
solution.why_others_wrong: (3/4)A divides by the old ω, forgetting that the mass change also changes ω; A assumes the amplitude is unaffected; (9/16)A squares the velocity ratio.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Oscillations', oscillations due to a spring; 'Laws of Motion', conservation of momentum
solution.final_answer: Option B: (√3/2)A

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Two particles execute simple harmonic motions x₁ = A sin ωt and x₂ = A sin(ωt + π/3) along the same straight line, about the same mean position. The maximum distance between the two particles during the motion is:

solution.concept: Superposing two SHMs of the same frequency
solution.explanation: Their separation is x₂ − x₁ = A[sin(ωt + π/3) − sin ωt] = 2A cos(ωt + π/6) sin(π/6) = A cos(ωt + π/6). It is itself simple harmonic with amplitude 2A sin(Δφ/2) = A.
solution.shortcut: Maximum separation = 2A sin(Δφ/2).
solution.why_others_wrong: 2A would need opposite phase (Δφ = π); √3 A uses 2A cos(Δφ/2), the amplitude of the SUM x₁ + x₂; A/2 uses A sin(Δφ/2) without the factor 2.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Oscillations', simple harmonic motion (phase)
solution.final_answer: Option C: A

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
A simple pendulum of length 1 m, at a place where g = π² m/s², is pulled aside through 4° and released. Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) Its period is 2 s.
(b) If it were released from 2° instead, its period would still be very nearly 2 s.
(c) As the bob passes through the mean position, the tension in the string is equal to the weight of the bob.
(d) If the length were made 4 m, the period would become 4 s.
(e) If the mass of the bob were doubled, the period would become √2 times as long.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Simple pendulum: period, and tension at the mean position
solution.explanation: For small angles T = 2π√(L/g), independent of amplitude and of the mass of the bob. At the mean position the bob is moving along a circular arc with speed v, so the string must supply a net upward force mv²/L: T − mg = mv²/L, and the tension exceeds the weight.
steps: (b) small angles → T independent of amplitude, true
(c) T = mg + mv²/L > mg, since v ≠ 0 at the mean position → false
(e) T does not depend on mass → false
solution.why_others_wrong: (c) treats the moving bob as if it were hanging at rest, forgetting the centripetal force mv²/L; (e) wrongly brings in the mass, which cancels in the restoring-force equation.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Oscillations', the simple pendulum
solution.final_answer: Option A: (a), (b) and (d) only

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
A stationary wave on a string is described by y = 0.04 sin(5πx) cos(200πt), where x and y are in metres and t in seconds. Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) The wavelength of the component travelling waves is 0.4 m.
(b) The frequency of oscillation of the particles is 100 Hz.
(c) The speed of each component travelling wave is 0.025 m/s.
(d) The amplitude of each component travelling wave is 0.04 m.
(e) There are nodes at x = 0, x = 0.2 m and x = 0.4 m.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: y = 2a sin kx cos ωt is the superposition of two waves of amplitude a travelling in opposite directions. Here k = 5π m⁻¹ and ω = 200π rad/s. Nodes are where sin kx = 0.
steps: (c) v = ω/k = 40 m/s, not 0.025 m/s (that is k/ω) → false
(d) 2a = 0.04 m → each wave has a = 0.02 m → false
solution.why_others_wrong: (c) inverts ω/k; (d) takes the amplitude at an antinode, 2a, as the amplitude of each component wave.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Waves', reflection of waves (standing waves and normal modes)
solution.final_answer: Option B: (a), (b) and (e) only

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A capacitor holds a charge of 240 μC when a potential difference of 60 V is applied across it. If the potential difference is raised to 90 V, the charge it holds becomes:

solution.concept: Capacitance C = Q/V is fixed by the geometry and the medium, so Q is proportional to V
solution.explanation: The capacitance found from the first reading stays the same when the voltage changes; only the charge changes.
steps: New charge Q = CV = 4 μF × 90 V = 360 μC
solution.why_others_wrong: 160 μC scales the charge by 60/90 instead of 90/60. 240 μC assumes the charge stays fixed. 540 μC scales the charge with V², which is how the stored energy (not the charge) changes.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance', capacitors and capacitance
solution.final_answer: Option A: 360 μC

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Ten identical capacitors are first connected all in parallel and then all in series. The ratio of the equivalent capacitance of the parallel combination to that of the series combination is:

solution.concept: Parallel: C_p = sum of capacitances; series: 1/C_s = sum of reciprocals
solution.explanation: For n identical capacitors C, the parallel combination is nC and the series combination is C/n.
solution.shortcut: For n identical capacitors the ratio is n².
solution.why_others_wrong: 1/100 is the series-to-parallel ratio, inverted. 10 compares only one of the combinations with a single capacitor. 1 assumes the arrangement does not matter.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance', combination of capacitors
solution.final_answer: Option B: 100

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A student applies Gauss's law to a system of discrete point charges. Which of the following is a correct guideline for choosing the Gaussian surface?

options.text: It must be a sphere centred on one of the charges
It must be the surface of a real conductor
It must not pass through any of the discrete point charges
It must enclose all the charges, because charges outside change the total flux through it

solution.concept: Gauss's law and the Gaussian surface
solution.explanation: Any closed surface may be used as a Gaussian surface, of any shape or size, real or imaginary. The one caution NCERT gives is that the surface should not pass through a discrete charge, because the electric field of a system of point charges is not well defined at the location of a charge.
steps: Field undefined at a point charge → surface must not pass through one
solution.why_others_wrong: The sphere is only a convenient choice when there is spherical symmetry; Gauss's law holds for any shape. The surface may be imaginary. Charges outside the surface contribute zero total flux (they change the field on the surface, but not the net flux).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electric Charges and Fields', Gauss's law
solution.final_answer: Option C: It must not pass through any of the discrete point charges

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): To find the electric field produced by a source charge, the force is measured on a test charge that is made vanishingly small.
Reason (R): A test charge that is not small could push or pull the source charges and disturb their arrangement, so the field measured would not be the field of the original arrangement.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Definition of the electric field using a test charge
solution.explanation: The field at a point is E = F/q for a test charge q placed there. If q were large, the force it exerts on the source charges could move them (or, on a conductor, redistribute them), so the field being measured would be changed by the act of measuring it. Making q negligibly small avoids this. R is exactly why A is done.
steps: A: test charge made vanishingly small → true
R: a large test charge disturbs the source arrangement → true
R gives the reason for A
solution.why_others_wrong: R is not an unrelated fact: it is the very reason the test charge must be small, so the 'NOT the correct explanation' option fails.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electric Charges and Fields', electric field
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: An electron moves from a point where the electrostatic potential is 20 V to a point where it is 70 V. Taking e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, the work done on the electron by the electric field is:

solution.concept: Work done by the field = −(change in potential energy) = −q(V_final − V_initial)
solution.explanation: The potential energy of a charge q at potential V is qV. For the electron q = −e, so moving to a higher potential lowers its potential energy, and the field does positive work on it.
solution.shortcut: A negative charge moving towards higher potential gains kinetic energy: |W| = e × 50 V = 50 eV, positive.
solution.why_others_wrong: −8.0 × 10⁻¹⁸ J treats the electron as a positive charge (or gives the work of an external agent). +1.12 × 10⁻¹⁷ J uses the final potential (70 V) alone. +1.44 × 10⁻¹⁷ J adds the two potentials instead of taking their difference.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance', potential energy of a charge in an external field
solution.final_answer: Option D: +8.0 × 10⁻¹⁸ J

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Point charges, each of +2 μC, are placed at five of the six corners of a regular hexagon of side 30 cm, in air; the sixth corner is empty. Taking 1/(4πε₀) = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻², the electric field at the centre of the hexagon is:

options.text: 2 × 10⁵ N/C, directed towards the empty corner
2 × 10⁵ N/C, directed away from the empty corner
1 × 10⁶ N/C, directed towards the empty corner

solution.explanation: If all six corners carried +2 μC, the fields at the centre would cancel in pairs (opposite corners). So the field of the five charges equals minus the field that the missing sixth charge would produce. A +2 μC charge at the empty corner would give a field at the centre pointing away from that corner; the actual field therefore points towards the empty corner. In a regular hexagon each corner is at a distance equal to the side from the centre.
steps: Distance of each corner from the centre = side = 0.30 m
Field of one charge there = 9 × 10⁹ × 2 × 10⁻⁶ / 0.09 = 2 × 10⁵ N/C
Five charges = six charges (zero) − one charge → 2 × 10⁵ N/C towards the empty corner
solution.shortcut: Field of the gap = field of a −2 μC charge placed at the empty corner.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Away from the empty corner' gets the magnitude right but reverses the direction. 1 × 10⁶ N/C adds the five magnitudes as if all the fields were parallel. Zero assumes the five charges are still symmetric.
solution.final_answer: Option A: 2 × 10⁵ N/C, directed towards the empty corner

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Two protons are a distance r apart in vacuum. Taking 1/(4πε₀) = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻², G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻², e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C and the proton mass as 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, the ratio of the electrostatic force between them to the gravitational force between them is about:

options.text: 1.2 × 10³⁶ at r = 1 m, and larger at smaller r

solution.concept: Coulomb's law and Newton's law of gravitation are both inverse-square laws
solution.explanation: Both forces vary as 1/r², so r cancels in the ratio: F_e/F_G = ke²/(Gm²).
solution.why_others_wrong: 8.1 × 10⁻³⁷ is the gravitational-to-electrostatic ratio. 2.1 × 10⁹ forgets to square the mass. The last option wrongly makes the ratio depend on r, although both forces fall off as 1/r².
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electric Charges and Fields', Coulomb's law
solution.final_answer: Option C: 1.2 × 10³⁶, whatever the value of r

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: An isolated parallel plate capacitor carries charges +40 μC and −40 μC on its plates. A slab of dielectric constant 5 is slid in so that it completely fills the space between the plates. The magnitude of the charge induced (by polarisation) on each face of the slab is:

solution.concept: Polarisation of a dielectric: induced surface charge reduces the field to E₀/K
solution.explanation: The free charge Q on the plates stays 40 μC (the capacitor is isolated). The face of the slab next to the positive plate acquires a charge −Q_p and the other face +Q_p. The field inside the slab is due to the net charge Q − Q_p, and it must be 1/K of the field without the slab.
solution.why_others_wrong: 8 μC is Q/K, the net (free minus induced) charge, not the induced charge. 200 μC multiplies by K; the induced charge can never exceed the free charge. 40 μC would cancel the field inside completely, which happens in a conductor, not a dielectric.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance', dielectrics and polarisation
solution.final_answer: Option D: 32 μC

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A 20 pF parallel plate capacitor with air between its plates is charged to 100 V and then disconnected from the battery. Its plates are now slowly pulled apart until their separation is doubled. The work done by the agent pulling the plates apart is:

solution.concept: With the battery disconnected the charge stays constant; U = Q²/(2C)
solution.explanation: Doubling the separation halves the capacitance. With Q fixed, the stored energy Q²/(2C) doubles. The plates attract each other, so the agent does positive work, equal to the increase in stored energy.
steps: Initial energy U = ½CV² = ½ × 20 × 10⁻¹² × 100² = 1 × 10⁻⁷ J
C → C/2 with Q fixed → U → 2U = 2 × 10⁻⁷ J
solution.why_others_wrong: 2 × 10⁻⁷ J is the final stored energy, not the increase. −5 × 10⁻⁸ J treats the voltage as fixed (as if the battery stayed connected), which would halve the energy. The work is not zero: the attracting plates must be pulled apart.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance', energy stored in a capacitor
solution.final_answer: Option B: 1 × 10⁻⁷ J

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (physical quantity) with List-II (its dimensional formula). A stands for the dimension of electric current.

List-I:
A. Electric field
B. Electric potential
C. Capacitance
D. Permittivity of free space, ε₀

List-II:
I. [M⁻¹ L⁻³ T⁴ A²]
II. [M L T⁻³ A⁻¹]
III. [M⁻¹ L⁻² T⁴ A²]
IV. [M L² T⁻³ A⁻¹]

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Dimensions from defining relations: E = F/q, V = W/q, C = Q/V, ε₀ = C d/A
solution.explanation: Charge has dimensions [A T]. E = F/q = [M L T⁻²]/[A T] = [M L T⁻³ A⁻¹]. V = W/q = [M L² T⁻²]/[A T] = [M L² T⁻³ A⁻¹]. C = Q/V = [A T]/[M L² T⁻³ A⁻¹] = [M⁻¹ L⁻² T⁴ A²]. ε₀ = Cd/A has one more L⁻¹ than C: [M⁻¹ L⁻³ T⁴ A²] (its unit is F/m).
solution.why_others_wrong: Swapping E and V confuses N/C with J/C (they differ by one power of length). Swapping C and ε₀ forgets that ε₀ is capacitance per unit length (F/m).
solution.final_answer: Option C: A-II, B-IV, C-III, D-I

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Two large, thin, parallel plane sheets carry the same uniform surface charge density +σ. In the region between the sheets (away from the edges), the electric field is zero.
Statement II: For the same two sheets, the electric field in the region outside them (away from the edges) has magnitude σ/(2ε₀).

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Field of a large plane sheet, σ/(2ε₀), and superposition
solution.explanation: Each sheet produces a field of magnitude σ/(2ε₀) directed away from it on both sides. Between the sheets the two fields are opposite and cancel, so Statement I is true. Outside, both fields point the same way and add to σ/ε₀, so Statement II is false.
steps: Outside: σ/(2ε₀) + σ/(2ε₀) = σ/ε₀ → II false
solution.why_others_wrong: σ/(2ε₀) is the field of a single sheet; outside two like sheets the fields add.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electric Charges and Fields', applications of Gauss's law: field due to a uniformly charged infinite plane sheet
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
An electric dipole of dipole moment p is placed in a non-uniform electric field E. Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) In general, the dipole experiences both a net force and a torque.
(b) If p is parallel to E, the net force on the dipole is in the direction of increasing field.
(c) If p is antiparallel to E, the net force on the dipole is in the direction of decreasing field.
(d) If p is parallel to E, the torque on the dipole is maximum.
(e) If p is antiparallel to E, the torque on the dipole is maximum.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Dipole in a non-uniform field: torque p × E and a net force that depends on how E varies
solution.explanation: In a non-uniform field the forces qE on the two charges are unequal, so there is in general a net force as well as a torque. With p parallel to E the dipole is pulled towards the stronger field; with p antiparallel it is pushed towards the weaker field (NCERT states both). The torque p × E has magnitude pE sin θ, which is zero (not maximum) when p is parallel or antiparallel to E.
solution.why_others_wrong: Any option containing (d) or (e) treats the aligned positions as positions of maximum torque; the torque is maximum when p is perpendicular to E.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electric Charges and Fields', dipole in a uniform external field
solution.final_answer: Option B: (a), (b) and (c) only

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Two point charges, each of +8 μC, are fixed at x = 0 and x = 2a on the x-axis. A third point charge q is placed at x = a. For all three charges to be in equilibrium under their mutual electrostatic forces alone, q must be:

solution.concept: Equilibrium of a system of charges: net Coulomb force on each charge zero
solution.explanation: The middle charge is in equilibrium for any q, by symmetry. For the charge at x = 0, the repulsion from the other +8 μC charge (distance 2a) must be balanced by an attraction towards the middle charge (distance a), so q must be negative.
steps: Force on the end charge from the other end: k(8)(8)/(2a)² = 16k/a² (away)
Force from q: k(8)|q|/a² (towards q, if q is negative)
solution.shortcut: q = −Q/4 for equal charges Q at the ends.
solution.why_others_wrong: +2 μC has the right size but would repel the end charges. −8 μC ignores that the middle charge is at half the distance. −4 μC uses distances a and 2a without squaring them.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electric Charges and Fields', forces between multiple charges
solution.final_answer: Option D: −2 μC

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A total charge of 5 nC is shared between two thin concentric conducting spherical shells of radii 10 cm and 20 cm (kept insulated from each other) so that the two shells have equal surface charge densities. Taking 1/(4πε₀) = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻², the electric potential at the common centre is:

solution.concept: Potential due to a charged spherical shell; superposition of potentials
solution.explanation: Equal surface densities mean the charges are in the ratio of the areas, r₁² : r₂² = 1 : 4, so the shells carry 1 nC and 4 nC. Inside a shell its potential is constant and equal to kQ/R, so at the centre each shell contributes kQ/R.
steps: Q₁ : Q₂ = 10² : 20² = 1 : 4 → Q₁ = 1 nC, Q₂ = 4 nC
solution.why_others_wrong: 450 V puts the whole 5 nC on the inner shell. 405 V divides the charge in the inverse ratio (4 nC on the inner shell). 225 V puts all the charge on the outer shell.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance', potential due to a system of charges
solution.final_answer: Option A: 270 V

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A 5 μF capacitor charged to 200 V is disconnected from the battery and connected across an uncharged capacitor of unknown capacitance. The common potential difference across the two capacitors settles at 40 V. The energy dissipated (as heat and radiation) during the redistribution of charge is:

solution.concept: Conservation of charge when capacitors are connected; stored energy ½CV²
solution.explanation: Charge is conserved: 5 μF × 200 V = 1000 μC is shared between the two capacitors at 40 V, so the total capacitance is 25 μF and the unknown capacitor is 20 μF. The energy lost is the initial stored energy minus the final stored energy.
steps: Q = 5 μF × 200 V = 1000 μC; total C = 1000/40 = 25 μF → unknown C = 20 μF
solution.shortcut: Loss = ½ [C₁C₂/(C₁ + C₂)] V₁² = ½ × 4 μF × (200 V)² = 0.08 J.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.02 J is the energy finally stored. 0.1 J is the energy initially stored. 0.016 J is the energy finally stored in the 20 μF capacitor alone.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance', energy stored in a capacitor
solution.final_answer: Option C: 0.08 J

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): When a dielectric slab that completely fills the space between the plates is inserted into an air-filled parallel plate capacitor that remains connected to a battery, the electric field between the plates does not change.
Reason (R): With the battery connected, the potential difference V between the plates and the plate separation d both stay the same, and the uniform field between the plates is E = V/d.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Capacitor with a dielectric: which quantity is held fixed
solution.explanation: The familiar result that a dielectric reduces the field to E₀/K applies when the charge is fixed (isolated capacitor). With the battery connected, V is fixed; the field in the filled gap is V/d, so it cannot change. The battery supplies extra charge (K times the original) so that the field of the free charges, reduced by the polarisation charges, is again V/d. R states exactly why A holds.
steps: A: V fixed, d fixed → E = V/d unchanged → true
R: true, and it is the reason for A
solution.why_others_wrong: Students who apply E₀/K regardless of the battery would mark A false; that rule needs the charge to be fixed. R is not an unrelated fact; it is the derivation of A.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance', effect of dielectric on capacitance
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A 50 μF capacitor already charged to 4 V is connected, through a resistor and with like terminals joined, to a 12 V battery of negligible internal resistance, and is left until it is fully charged to 12 V. The heat produced in the resistor during this process is:

solution.concept: Energy balance in charging: work done by the battery = increase in stored energy + heat
solution.explanation: The battery moves the extra charge ΔQ = C(12 − 4) through its emf of 12 V, so it does work ΔQ × 12 V. Only part of this goes into the capacitor's stored energy; the rest is dissipated in the resistor.
steps: ΔQ = 50 μF × 8 V = 400 μC; battery work = 400 μC × 12 V = 4.8 mJ
Increase in stored energy = ½ × 50 μF × (12² − 4²) V² = 3.2 mJ
solution.shortcut: Heat = ½C(ΔV)² = ½ × 50 μF × 8² = 1.6 mJ when a battery tops up a capacitor through a resistor.
solution.why_others_wrong: 3.2 mJ is the increase in stored energy. 4.8 mJ is the work done by the battery. 2.4 mJ assumes that half of the battery's work always becomes heat, which is true only when the capacitor starts uncharged.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance', energy stored in a capacitor
solution.final_answer: Option B: 1.6 mJ

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: An electric bulb is rated 100 W, 220 V. Treating its resistance as constant, the resistance of its filament when it is working at its rated voltage is:

solution.explanation: At its rated voltage the bulb draws its rated power, so R = V²/P.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2.2 Ω is V/P, which has no physical meaning here. 0.45 is P/V, the current in amperes, not a resistance. 22 kΩ multiplies V by P.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', electrical energy, power
solution.final_answer: Option C: 484 Ω

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A current of 6 A enters a parallel combination of a 2 Ω resistor and a 4 Ω resistor. The current through the 4 Ω resistor is:

solution.concept: In a parallel combination the potential difference is the same, so the current divides in inverse proportion to the resistances
solution.explanation: The equivalent resistance is 2 × 4/(2 + 4) = 4/3 Ω, so the common potential difference is 6 A × 4/3 Ω = 8 V.
steps: Current in 4 Ω = 8/4 = 2 A (and 4 A in the 2 Ω resistor)
solution.shortcut: I₄ = I × R₂/(R₂ + R₄) = 6 × 2/6 = 2 A.
solution.why_others_wrong: 4 A is the current in the 2 Ω resistor (the larger share goes through the smaller resistance). 3 A assumes an equal split. 6 A treats the resistors as if they were in series.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', combination of resistors - series and parallel
solution.final_answer: Option A: 2 A

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The current through a metal wire is doubled, and at the same time the wire is replaced by another wire of the same metal (at the same temperature) with half the cross-sectional area. The drift speed of the free electrons becomes:

solution.concept: I = n e A v_d, so v_d = I/(n e A)
solution.explanation: The number density n of free electrons is a property of the metal and does not change. The drift speed is proportional to I and inversely proportional to A.
solution.why_others_wrong: '2 times' accounts for the doubled current but not the smaller area. 'The same' assumes the two changes cancel. '1/4' inverts the dependence on both I and A.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', drift of electrons and the origin of resistivity
solution.final_answer: Option D: 4 times the original value

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Although the drift speed of the free electrons in a copper wire is only of the order of 1 mm/s, a wire of cross-sectional area 1 mm² can carry a current of several amperes.
Reason (R): The number density of free electrons in a metal such as copper is very large, of the order of 10²⁸ to 10²⁹ per cubic metre.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Current in terms of drift speed: I = n e A v_d
solution.explanation: The current through a cross-section is the charge carried across it per second, n e A v_d. With n ≈ 8.5 × 10²⁸ m⁻³, e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, A = 10⁻⁶ m² and v_d = 10⁻³ m/s, I ≈ 14 A. A tiny drift speed still gives a sizeable current only because n is enormous, so R explains A.
steps: I = n e A v_d: small v_d is compensated by very large n → R explains A
solution.why_others_wrong: R is not a separate property: the large n is exactly what makes the current large in spite of the small drift speed.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', drift of electrons and the origin of resistivity
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The resistivity of a metal wire at a given temperature increases if the wire is made longer.
Statement II: The SI unit of conductance, the reciprocal of resistance, is the siemens (S), with 1 S = 1 Ω⁻¹.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Resistance depends on dimensions; resistivity is a property of the material
solution.explanation: R = ρl/A depends on the length and area, but ρ depends only on the material and its temperature, so Statement I is false. Conductance G = 1/R is measured in siemens, 1 S = 1 Ω⁻¹, so Statement II is true.
steps: I: a longer wire has more resistance, not more resistivity → false
II: G = 1/R, unit S = Ω⁻¹ → true
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement I confuses resistance with resistivity.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', Ohm's law; resistivity
solution.final_answer: Option D: Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Three identical bulbs, connected in series across a supply of constant voltage, together consume a power P. Treating the resistance of each bulb as constant, the total power they consume when they are connected in parallel across the same supply is:

solution.concept: For a fixed supply voltage, total power = V²/R_eq
solution.explanation: In series the equivalent resistance is 3R; in parallel it is R/3, which is 9 times smaller. With V fixed, power is inversely proportional to the equivalent resistance.
solution.why_others_wrong: 3P compares the parallel combination with a single bulb's resistance R. P/9 inverts the ratio. P assumes the arrangement does not matter.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', electrical energy, power
solution.final_answer: Option B: 9P

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A uniform wire of resistance 18 Ω is bent into the shape of an equilateral triangle ABC, its ends being joined. The resistance between the corner A and the midpoint M of the opposite side BC is:

solution.concept: Resistance proportional to length; parallel combination
solution.explanation: Each side is 6 Ω, and half a side is 3 Ω. From A to M there are two identical paths: A → B → M and A → C → M, each of 6 + 3 = 9 Ω. These two paths are in parallel.
steps: Each side 6 Ω; BM = MC = 3 Ω
Each path A→B→M or A→C→M = 9 Ω
Two 9 Ω paths in parallel = 4.5 Ω
solution.why_others_wrong: 9 Ω takes only one of the two paths. 4 Ω is the resistance between two corners (6 Ω in parallel with 12 Ω). 6 Ω is just the resistance of one side.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', combination of resistors - series and parallel
solution.final_answer: Option D: 4.5 Ω

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Two wires X and Y are made of the same metal and have the same mass. The length of Y is twice that of X. The two wires are connected in series across a battery. The ratio of the heat produced per second in X to that in Y is:

solution.concept: R = ρl/A, with equal mass (equal volume) fixing A = volume/l; in series, heat ∝ R
solution.explanation: Same metal and same mass means the same volume V. The cross-sectional area is A = V/l, so R = ρl/A = ρl²/V, i.e. R ∝ l². In series the same current flows through both, so the heat per second I²R is proportional to R.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1 : 2 uses R ∝ l and forgets that the longer wire is also thinner. 4 : 1 is the ratio for a parallel connection, where heat ∝ 1/R. 1 : 8 cubes the length ratio.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', resistivity of various materials; electrical energy, power
solution.final_answer: Option B: 1 : 4

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
A cell has emf 6 V and internal resistance 1 Ω. Match each situation in List-I with the potential difference between the terminals of the cell in List-II.

List-I:
A. No current is drawn from the cell (open circuit)
B. The terminals are joined directly by a thick wire of negligible resistance
C. A 2 Ω resistor is connected across the terminals
D. The cell is being charged by an external source, the charging current being 2 A

List-II:
I. 8 V
II. 0 V
III. 6 V
IV. 4 V

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Terminal potential difference V = ε − Ir while discharging and V = ε + Ir while charging
solution.explanation: Open circuit: no current, so V = ε = 6 V. Short circuit: the terminals are at the same potential, V = 0 (the current ε/r = 6 A makes Ir = ε). With 2 Ω: I = 6/3 = 2 A and V = 6 − 2 × 1 = 4 V. While charging, the current enters the positive terminal and V = ε + Ir = 6 + 2 = 8 V.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes either give the charging case ε − Ir (4 V), or give the short-circuited cell its emf, although its terminals are joined by a wire of negligible resistance.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', cells, emf, internal resistance
solution.final_answer: Option B: A-III, B-II, C-IV, D-I

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A 4 Ω resistor is connected in series with a parallel combination of a 6 Ω resistor and a 12 Ω resistor, and the arrangement is connected across a battery. In which resistor is heat produced at the greatest rate?

options.text: The 6 Ω and 12 Ω resistors equally, since they have the same potential difference

solution.concept: Heat produced per second = I²R; current division in a parallel combination
solution.explanation: Let the current through the 4 Ω resistor be I. It divides in inverse ratio of the resistances: 2I/3 through 6 Ω and I/3 through 12 Ω. The heating rates are 4I², 6(2I/3)² = 8I²/3 and 12(I/3)² = 4I²/3.
solution.why_others_wrong: The 6 Ω resistor gets more heat than the 12 Ω one (same V, so heat ∝ 1/R), but still less than the 4 Ω resistor, which carries the full current. The 12 Ω resistor gets the least. Equal potential difference does not mean equal heat when the resistances differ.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', electrical energy, power
solution.final_answer: Option A: The 4 Ω resistor

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): A voltmeter of very high resistance connected directly across the terminals of a cell reads very nearly the emf of the cell.
Reason (R): Such a voltmeter draws a negligible current, so the potential drop across the internal resistance of the cell is negligible.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.explanation: The terminal voltage differs from the emf by the drop Ir across the internal resistance. A voltmeter of very high resistance R_V draws a current ε/(R_V + r), which is tiny, so Ir is tiny and the reading is almost ε. R gives the reason for A.
steps: I ≈ 0 for a very high resistance voltmeter → V ≈ ε
solution.why_others_wrong: R is the direct reason for A; it is not an unrelated statement.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', cells, emf, internal resistance
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The resistance of a metal wire is 50 Ω at 0 °C and 70 Ω at 100 °C. Assuming that the resistance varies linearly with temperature, the temperature at which its resistance is 61 Ω is:

solution.concept: R_t = R₀(1 + αt) for a linear variation
solution.explanation: The resistance rises by 20 Ω over 100 °C, i.e. 0.2 Ω per °C. A rise of 11 Ω above the 0 °C value therefore needs 55 °C.
solution.why_others_wrong: 87 °C takes R/R₁₀₀ × 100. 122 °C takes R/R₀ × 100. 45 °C measures the 11 Ω step down from 100 °C instead of up from 0 °C.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', temperature dependence of resistivity
solution.final_answer: Option D: 55 °C

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Twelve identical resistors, each of 5 Ω, form a wheel: six of them make the sides of a regular hexagon (the rim) and the other six join each corner of the hexagon to its centre O (the spokes). The equivalent resistance between two diametrically opposite corners of the hexagon is:

solution.concept: Symmetry of a network and Kirchhoff's junction rule
solution.explanation: Hold corner 1 at potential V and the opposite corner 4 at 0. By symmetry the centre O is at V/2, corners 2 and 6 (next to 1) are at a common potential x, and corners 3 and 5 are at V − x. Apply the junction rule at corner 2, which is joined to 1, to 3 and to O.
steps: At corner 2: (V − x) + ((V − x) − x) + (V/2 − x) = 0 → x = 5V/8
Current leaving corner 1 (each resistor 5 Ω): [2(V − 5V/8) + (V − V/2)]/5 = (5V/4)/5 = V/4
solution.why_others_wrong: 7.5 Ω uses only the two rim paths (15 Ω each, in parallel). 30/7 Ω adds the 10 Ω spoke path through O in parallel with the rim but ignores the spokes to the other corners, which carry current. 10 Ω uses the spoke path alone.
solution.final_answer: Option B: 4 Ω

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: In a metre bridge with a 10 Ω standard resistor in the right gap, the null point is 50.0 cm from the left end when a resistor X is in the left gap, and 60.0 cm from the left end when X is replaced by a resistor Y. When X and Y are connected in parallel and placed together in the left gap (10 Ω still in the right gap), the null point will be at a distance from the left end of:

solution.concept: Metre bridge balance: X/R = l/(100 − l)
solution.explanation: The two separate balances give X and Y; their parallel combination is then balanced against the same 10 Ω.
solution.why_others_wrong: 71.4 cm uses X and Y in series (25 Ω). 55.0 cm simply averages the two balance lengths. 62.5 cm is the correct balance length measured from the wrong (right-hand) end.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', Wheatstone bridge
solution.final_answer: Option C: 37.5 cm

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A uniform wire of resistance 9 Ω is stretched uniformly to three times its original length, its volume and resistivity remaining unchanged. It is then cut into three pieces of equal length, and the three pieces are connected in parallel. The resistance of the combination is:

solution.concept: R = ρl/A with volume constant gives R ∝ l²; identical resistors in parallel
solution.explanation: Stretching to three times the length at constant volume reduces the area to one third, so the resistance becomes 3² = 9 times larger. Each third of the stretched wire then has one third of that resistance, and three equal resistors in parallel give one third of one piece.
steps: Three 27 Ω pieces in parallel: 27/3 = 9 Ω
solution.why_others_wrong: 1 Ω ignores the stretching (pieces of 3 Ω in parallel). 27 Ω is the resistance of one piece. 3 Ω uses R ∝ l for the stretching, forgetting that the area also decreases.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', Ohm's law; resistivity
solution.final_answer: Option A: 9 Ω

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
In a Wheatstone bridge, resistors P and Q form one branch and R and S the other; both branches are connected across a cell of emf ε and internal resistance r, and a galvanometer joins the P–Q junction to the R–S junction. The bridge is balanced. Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) No current flows through the galvanometer.
(b) The balance condition P/Q = R/S does not depend on the emf of the cell.
(c) The balance condition does not depend on the resistance of the galvanometer.
(d) The balance condition depends on the internal resistance of the cell.
(e) If the galvanometer is replaced by a resistor of any value, the currents through P, Q, R and S do not change.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Balanced Wheatstone bridge: the two junctions are at the same potential
